arXiv:2611.22368v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Changing the holding reference during a fixed-duration wait can reverse the ranking of visual recovery methods. We introduce AuditEmbodied, a paired execution and trajectory evaluation framework that independently varies holding references and waiting duration while keeping recovery executors frozen. A 960-execution factorial on 20 initialization seeds compares CAD-feedback and landmark-based recovery from identical post-wait physical states within each holding and waiting condition. Protected completion requires successful recovery under the declared execution constraints. At a 1 s wait with registered wrist references, their protected completion counts change from 6/40 versus 19/40 under registered holding to 34/40 versus 22/40 under position-only holding. Trajectory analysis localizes the main separation to grasp formation: small observation-time target residuals precede large tracking errors. Joint diagnostics and controlled interventions characterize persistent tracking constraints. On fresh seeds, gradual position reanchoring improves CAD recovery's long-wait completion by 42.5 percentage points and reduces mean complete recovery time by 6.06 s relative to registered holding. Additional evaluations with pretrained policies, handover, and a mass-matched geometry characterize holding-reference sensitivity across executors and physical regimes. These findings establish holding reference as an explicit evaluation condition for comparing visual recovery performance.

Industry News: Testing changes, fast: Introducing agentic assessments in Database Center

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that applying recommendations to a production database can feel risky if you can’t easily quantify the performance benefit or justify the additional cost.
  • Sources indicate that to help solve this problem, we’re excited to announce the preview of assessments in Database Center for Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL.
  • Managing production databases means balancing system stability, performance, and infrastructure spend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

It has been revealed that applying recommendations to a production database can feel risky if you can’t easily quantify the performance benefit or justify the additional cost. While Database Center flags fleet-level health issues and provides proactive recommendations, database administrators still face the challenge of testing recommended changes without disrupting live applications or spending hours manually configuring staging replicas.

Sources indicate that to help solve this problem, we’re excited to announce the preview of assessments in Database Center for Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. Assessments is an agentic workflow that lets you run automated, isolated synthetic benchmarks on cloned instances, helping you verify potential performance gains before touching your production environment.

Managing production databases means balancing system stability, performance, and infrastructure spend. When Database Center alerts you to a potential bottleneck and recommends a change, you need to evaluate the change before you can implement it. That workflow can be complex:.

Setting up dedicated staging environments to mirror production settings.

Running benchmark workloads to simulate real-world traffic.

Measuring latency, throughput, and resource saturation before and after applying changes.

Calculating whether performance gains justify potential cost adjustments.

Because this manual benchmarking process takes a lot of time and engineering effort, it’s easy to put off making critical updates, leaving databases under-provisioned or inefficient.

Sources indicate that assessments simplify performance validation by automating the entire testing cycle in an isolated environment. When you click "Assess impact" on a supported recommendation in Database Center, the assessments workflow handles each step of the benchmarking process:.

Plan creation: Assessments builds a customized test plan for running a synthetic benchmark tailored to your instance. You can refine parameters such as client connections, transaction counts, query mode, or benchmark duration using plain-language prompts to match your target workload requirements (for example, "Change the benchmark duration to 60 seconds").

Safe isolation: The agentic workflow clones your primary instance so that benchmarks run without consuming production resources or affecting live traffic.

Baseline measurement: The workflow automatically runs synthetic workloads against the cloned instance to establish performance metrics from before the change.

Applying changes: The workflow modifies the cloned environment according to the selected recommendation.

Comparative reporting: Finally, it reruns the benchmark workload and generates an evaluation report comparing pre- and post-change metrics, including transaction throughput, average latency, CPU utilization, and memory usage — and automatically deletes the temporary clone once the assessment completes.

During the preview, you can run automated assessments for three types of Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL updates:.

Machine upgrade: Measure how increased vCPU and memory allocations impact query throughput and reduce compute contention under load.

Edition upgrade: Compare performance metrics between Cloud SQL Enterprise and Enterprise Plus editions to verify throughput gains and reduced latency.

Enable data cache: Evaluate how enabling data cache on Enterprise Plus instances affects read latency and offloads I/O bottlenecks for data-intensive workloads.

Assessments in Database Center are available in preview. You can start validating performance changes in your Cloud SQL for Postgres environment today directly in the Google Cloud console:.

Review the release notes for the latest updates on Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL.

Read the assessments overview to explore architecture details and supported database versions.

Follow the step-by-step guide to create an assessment for your instances in Database Center.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo. You can now serve models that are too large for a single instance, and keep token generation fast when prompts are long. You don't have to build or operate distributed serving infrastructure yourself. HyperPod manages Dynamo for you through the Inference Operator add-on.

According to recent reports, as models grow, two problems limit inference. A large model can need more GPU memory than one instance has. Long prompts also slow token generation, because the prefill and decode stages compete for the same GPUs. Until now, customers had to build and run their own distributed serving stack to work around both.

With Dynamo on HyperPod, you can run a single model across multiple nodes. You can also split prefill and decode into separate GPU pools that scale independently, so a long prompt no longer stalls token generation for other requests. KV-aware routing sends each request to a worker that already holds the relevant cached context. This cuts recomputation and raises throughput. HyperPod runs the underlying infrastructure: EFA networking, GPU capacity management, node replacement, endpoint registration, autoscaling, and observability. Your team can spend its time on the models instead.

To get started, bring your existing Dynamo manifests if you want full control. You can also use a simplified configuration that HyperPod translates into the underlying infrastructure.

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference with NVIDIA Dynamo support is available in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (N. California, Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt, Stockholm, Ireland, London, Spain), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Hyderabad, Singapore, Sydney, Jakarta, Melbourne, Tokyo), and South America (São Paulo). To learn more, see the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod documentation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

According to recent reports, structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

arXiv:2611.22338v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: We consider the problem of evaluating AI agents undertaking investment-research tasks, where agents interact with external information sources and computational tools to produce financial analyses and research reports. An crucial challenge is that the quality of an agent's final output does not necessarily reflect the quality of its execution process, while the reliability of the resulting assessment also depends on the validity of the evaluation procedure. Furthermore, investment-research tasks differ considerably in their requirements for numerical accuracy, information retrieval, financial analysis and supporting evidence, making it difficult to assess agent performance using a uniform set of criteria. We propose a domain-oriented evaluation framework that distinguishes outcome quality from execution quality and accommodates these differences through task-specific criteria, deterministic validators and independent large language model judges. We also introduce an evaluation-validity mechanism that examines the integrity of evaluation inputs, reference information, supporting evidence and grading outputs, with expert review used to resolve identified deficiencies and significant grading disagreements. Numerical results show that the proposed framework can distinguish differences in agent performance across evaluation dimensions, while identifying potential reliability challenges in the evaluation process. The associated implementation and evaluation materials will be made available on GitHub.

AWS now enables agentic coding harnesses to open the upcoming AWS sign-up experience for developers who don't have an AWS account yet. Previously, developers working in agentic coding environments like Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor had to manually navigate to aws.amazon.com, sign up for an AWS account and configure credentials before deploying workloads, interrupting the developer's experience. Now, developers can go from an idea to deploying a running application by the browser automatically opening, completing sign up and returning short-lived credentials to the harness. When developers sign up for AWS from their coding agent, they start with the new AWS experience. Their first project comes set up with a home Region, IAM role manager, and short-term credentials that refresh automatically, so the agent can start deploying right away. To try the new experience, configure the AWS Agent Toolkit in your agentic coding harness using the AWS MCP server setup guide or install the AWS Agent Toolkit plugin. On first authentication, you'll be prompted to open a browser directly to the AWS sign-up page. You can also initiate account creation via the AWS CLI by running aws signup (opens directly to sign-up) or aws login (opens the SignIn page with a Sign Up option). To learn more, see the AWS Agent Toolkit documentation or the AWS Account Documentation.

Multistage Contextual Optimization for Vehicle Repositioning

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (281 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ride-hailing platforms reposition idle vehicles to improve spatial supply-demand balances. This problem is prediction-driven and multistage: at each stage, the platform forecasts future demand, executes current decisions, and uses the resulting state to initialize the next stage. We formulate a multistage linear program (LP) with a macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) linking accumulation to trip completion. We then develop a multistage contextual optimization approach that uses decision performance to train the prediction model. The learning problem combines multiple coupled stages, context that depends on earlier decisions, and predictions that affect the objective, the constraint matrix, and the right-hand side of the LP. We derive the exact gradient, which has three parts: parameters change forecasts and hence decisions; earlier decisions change the current decision through the inherited state; and this state also changes forecasts as context. An equivalent adjoint uses reverse vector-Jacobian products, avoiding full solution and state-parameter Jacobians. Finally, forward propagation solves many stage LPs one after another, which makes training slow. We propose a parallel block evaluation algorithm that solves blocks of consecutive stages in parallel and repeatedly feeds each block output to the next block. We prove that the algorithm recovers the serial trajectory within a finite number of passes and that its gradient error remains bounded when it stops early. On New York City ride-hailing data, multistage contextual optimization yields 7.7% to 9.1% more business benefit than the same predictor trained by mean squared error, outperforms all compared baselines from five paradigms, and even outperforms realized demand fed to the same policy. With eight workers, parallel block evaluation shortens training by a factor of 1.86 without loss of decision performance.

#10026. Tech Report: NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

📅 03 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1551 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders.
  • Recent findings suggest that we fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach.
  • NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

Recent findings suggest that we fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

According to recent reports, many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

According to recent reports, neoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

It has been revealed that neoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:.

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:.

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

Recent findings suggest that one NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

In a recent development, we report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

In a recent development, late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:.

Industry observers note that we tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

People can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding new documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

Industry observers note that we provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers right now supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Sources indicate that visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:.

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

Industry observers note that neoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

Industry observers note that neoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Manufacturer for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

#10025. What’s new in OKF v0.3: enterprise-ready knowledge, use cases, and skills

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1635 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Google ↗ Open Full Page

What’s new in OKF v0.3: enterprise-ready knowledge, use cases, and skills

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1635 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in June we introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), an open specification that provides plain markdown and YAML to give agents the context they need.
  • Industry observers note that in production, bundles move between organizations, multiple agents edit the same corpus, and independent tools need to read a bundle the same way.
  • Recent findings suggest that we're also launching OKF use cases, which are community guides for using OKF alongside other industry standards, and two agent skills that let coding agents write and read OKF bundles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tech Lead, BigQuery, Engineering, Data Cloud.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

In a recent development, in June we introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), an open specification that provides plain markdown and YAML to give agents the context they need. In July, v0.2 added trust signals: provenance, trust, freshness, lifecycle, and attestation.

Industry observers note that in production, bundles move between organizations, multiple agents edit the same corpus, and independent tools need to read a bundle the same way. Released today, OKF v0.3 adds precise conformance rules, trust tiers that keep pace with agent edits, self-describing bundles with licensing, safe ways to retire and move knowledge, a stable extension model, and a clear versioning policy. However, the core idea behind OKF stays the same: type is still the only required field, and your existing bundles keep working.

Recent findings suggest that we're also launching OKF use cases, which are community guides for using OKF alongside other industry standards, and two agent skills that let coding agents write and read OKF bundles. Finally, to make cross-organization collaboration easier, we’re moving OKF out of the Google Cloud Platform GitHub org into a standalone organization at https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/.

Let’s take a closer look at what’s fresh in OKF v0.3.

In a recent development, v0.3 adds a formal conformance section, allowing independent producers and consumers to work together by design. The spec is self-contained and uses RFC 2119 keywords. It gives one clear answer to the questions that come up when tools from different teams and vendors read the same bundle. The full detail is in the spec, but a few themes matter for anyone building on OKF:.

Built on standard file formats. OKF uses a small, widely supported set of standards: YAML 1.2 frontmatter, CommonMark with GFM tables and footnotes, and RFC 3339 timestamps. If your tools handle those, they handle OKF.

OKF bundles share space with other markdown files. A .md file without a type is skipped by OKF consumers, so README.md, AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, and SKILL.md can live inside a bundle without breaking it. Files that aren't markdown, like images or attester code, are assets that concepts can link to.

Industry observers note that consumers handle real-world input predictably. Bundles written by many agents can contain nulls, empty strings, single values where a list was expected, and new vocabulary. v0.3 specifies how a consumer reads each of these. Consumers accept these inputs without failing, while validators log warnings for malformed entries. A bundle never fails because an optional field is missing or a link is broken.

v0.2 gave every concept a trust tier: unverified, machine-confirmed, or human-reviewed. As agents take on more of the editing, v0.3 makes sure the tier always reflects the latest version of the content. Here's a typical sequence:.

A person reviews a metric definition and signs off.

A week later, an agent refines the definition.

The trust tier now reflects that the person hasn't yet reviewed the latest text.

In v0.3, only current verifications count. A verification is current when it happened at or after the last meaningful change to the content, recorded in generated.at:.

This concept is now machine-confirmed, not human-reviewed, until a person confirms it again. The older sign-off stays in the file as history, and a UI can show it as "reviewed before the last change.".

In a recent development, v0.3 also standardizes actor identifiers. Actors are / for tools, or : for everything else, and v0.3 adds team: next to human: and process:. Only human: earns human-reviewed, because a team name doesn't say which person actually checked the content.

Recent findings suggest that when an agent has access to dozens of bundles, bundle-level metadata supports progressive disclosure so it can pick the right bundle without reading every file. In v0.3, the bundle-root index.md can carry frontmatter about the bundle itself:.

Sources indicate that description is written for routing. In one sentence it states what the bundle covers and when to use it.

license makes clear what you're allowed to do with knowledge you receive from someone else.

okf_version tells a consumer which rules to apply, including compatibility fallbacks for older bundles.

Tools that regenerate index.md must keep this frontmatter.

Knowledge evolves, and an agent that finds a deprecated concept should be able to get to its replacement. v0.3 adds superseded_by:.

Consumers that filter to current knowledge follow the pointer and return the replacement. The same mechanism handles moves and renames. Leave a short deprecated concept at the old path that points to the new one, and existing links and stored references keep working.

Links in the body and path fields in frontmatter (resource, superseded_by, executor.resource, and others) now resolve the same way:.

A value with a scheme (https:) is an absolute URL.

A value that starts with / resolves from the bundle root.

Anything else resolves from the directory of the file that contains it, just like on GitHub or in any markdown editor.

For bundles marked v0.2 or earlier, or with no version, a consumer can also resolve paths from the bundle root, so existing bundles keep working.

In a recent development, v0.3 also makes explicit that links are not parent/child relationships. Only the directory tree defines hierarchy. A link is an untyped, directed relationship, and the text around it notes what kind ("joins with," "replaces," "depends on"). Path fields that point at concepts are edges in the bundle graph too.

The community has been extending OKF since v0.1, with typed edges, routing hints, and erasure profiles. v0.3 makes a few extension mechanisms a first-class rule:.

Extension keys are allowed at any level, including inside sources entries, verified events, executor, and attester.

A producer that edits a file must keep the keys it doesn't understand so one tool doesn't overwrite metadata added by another.

Recent findings suggest that future OKF versions will never define keys that start with x-. Name your keys x--, for example x-acme-owner, and they won't collide with a future spec version.

Sources indicate that v0.3 defines OKF's versioning rules. Before 1.0, minor versions may include breaking changes as long as each is documented with a consumer fallback where possible. Starting at 1.0, minor versions will be strictly additive, and released normative text will not change in place.

Recent findings suggest that the spec also lists what was considered and deferred: typed relationships, the full attestation runtime protocol (receipt and verdict wire formats), semantic-layer attestation, validity windows, and a refuted verification event. Until the community agrees on a form for these, extension keys are the place to experiment. We'd like your proposals.

OKF keeps its core specification small and links to existing domain schemas like Avro, Protobuf, or OpenAPI instead of duplicating them. In practice, though, when your organization already has an established artifact in another standard, such as a schema, a contract, or a spec, what should the OKF concept next to it say, and how should an agent use the two together?

Recent findings suggest that starting with v0.3, we're publishing use cases: guides for using OKF with other industry standards. Each one explains:.

Where the boundary sits: what belongs in the other standard and what belongs in OKF.

How to link the two: which frontmatter and link conventions point from a concept into the other artifact.

What an agent should do with the combination.

A complete worked example you can copy.

It has been revealed that use cases are layered on the core spec, not part of it. A bundle that ignores them is still a conformant OKF bundle. When a convention proves itself across several use cases, it can be proposed for the core spec through the usual process.

Use cases are managed directly in GitHub. Each use case gets its own folder under usecases/ in the OKF repository, for example usecases//. The guide is a .md file in that folder, and any sample bundles or artifacts sit next to it. Use cases are reviewed, versioned, and discussed like any other change.

According to recent reports, if you pair OKF with a standard, please send us a proposal. A rough first draft is welcome. Open a pull request that adds a folder under usecases/ with a .md file in it, and we'll refine it together in review.

v0.3 has two breaking changes, and existing v0.2 bundles stay readable:.

Path fields resolve relative to their file. Fallback: for bundles marked v0.2 or earlier, or with no version, consumers can resolve from the bundle root.

Only current verifications count toward the trust tier. No fallback needed, since tiers can only go down.

Everything else is a clarification or an optional addition. v0.1 fallbacks (timestamp, body # Citations) still apply.

The two skills live in the new repository and follow the open Agent Skills format, so any agent that supports skills can load them.

okf-generate writes, updates, migrates, and validates bundles from available sources. It cites a source for each claim, records a human review only when that person confirms it, and copies attested computations from a sanctioned source instead of writing them.

Recent findings suggest that okf-consume answers questions from a bundle. For each concept used, it reports the trust tier, status, freshness, and attestation result, and runs attested computations only through the bundle's configured executor and attester.

To install them in Gemini CLI, run:.

The README lists the install steps for other agents.

It has been revealed that read the v0.3 spec. Add okf_version to your bundles, and check that your consumer computes trust tiers from current verifications only. Problems and pull requests, including fresh use case proposals, are welcome on GitHub.

Spec, samples, use cases, and reference implementations: https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/.

According to recent reports, AWS Cost Optimization Hub now lets you stop idle Amazon EC2 instances directly from your recommendations. Cost Optimization Hub consolidates and prioritizes cost optimization recommendations across your AWS accounts and Regions, including idle resources. Previously, stopping an idle instance required you to leave Cost Optimization Hub and identify the specific instance in the Amazon EC2 console. Now you can stop it from the Savings opportunities page in Cost Optimization Hub.

In a recent development, when you choose Stop next to an idle instance recommendation, a confirmation reveals the instance, its account and Region, what the instance loses when it stops, such as instance store data and data in memory, and what continues to bill, such as EBS volumes and Elastic IP addresses. Stopping does not terminate the instance or delete its EBS volumes, and you can start it again from the EC2 console. Stop needs no separate setup and uses your existing permissions. To receive idle resource recommendations, turn on Cost Optimization Hub and AWS Compute Optimizer.

This feature is available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions.

Sources indicate that to get started, open Cost Optimization Hub in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console and go to Savings opportunities. To learn more, see the Cost Optimization Hub product page and user guide.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.22310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite advances in LLM-based table reasoning, most studies focus on single-table settings. Multi-table QA requires multi-hop reasoning over complex table relationships and evidence dispersed across long contexts, often without verifiable intermediate traces. To address these challenges, we introduce EviDA, an evidence-centric dual-agent framework comprising an Evidence Construction Agent and a Reasoning and Answering Agent. The Evidence Construction Agent generates and executes table-manipulation programs over complete tables to produce question-specific evidence and verifiable intermediate traces, simplifying subsequent reasoning. The Reasoning and Answering Agent then performs multi-hop reasoning over this evidence to derive final answers. We further introduce EviDARL, which combines agent-specific fine-grained rewards with parameter-efficient alternating reinforcement learning to improve collaboration between the agents. By optimizing each agent in turn while holding the other fixed, EviDARL enables bidirectional adaptation between evidence construction and answer reasoning. Experiments on MMQA and TQA-Bench demonstrate that EviDARL substantially outperforms competitive open-model and multi-table reasoning baselines under constrained model and training budgets.

Sources indicate that amazon Connect Customer message templates, which personalize each message with details about its recipient, now support case fields from Cases and calculated attributes from Customer Profiles, such as a customer's most frequent contact channel. Companies that send updates about a claim, an order, or an application need each message to reflect that customer's record. Template authors can insert case fields, including custom fields that administrators define, and Connect Customer fills in the current value for each recipient every time it sends a message that uses the template.

It has been revealed that A claims manager at an insurance manufacturer can build one email template that pulls each claim's reference number and status from its case, so every policyholder receives an upgrade about their own claim. A retailer can add a custom calculated attribute, such as each customer's total orders in the past year, to a loyalty email so every customer sees their own count. Developers can pass these values when they render a template with the RenderMessageTemplate API.

Recent findings suggest that you can use case and calculated attributes in message templates in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London).

To learn more, see Add personalized content to message templates in the Amazon Connect Customer Administrator Guide.

Efficient Wide-Beam Generative Retrieval with Model-Native Trie Decoding and Shared-Context Attention

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (185 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.22309v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) predicts catalog entries as short semantic identifiers (SIDs). Trie-constrained beam search keeps these identifiers valid, but wide beams expose two serving costs: vocabulary-wide score tensors that are mostly discarded, and repeated attention over the same prompt. We present Trie-Head, a model-native output interface that stores the identifier trie as validated GPU tensors. Compared with a Python custom logit processor (CLP), it reduces CPU--GPU coordination and memory traffic by avoiding Python constraint callbacks and vocabulary-wide candidate buffers. It scores compact codebook candidates and streams the full-vocabulary normalizer, preserving the original model's valid-token scores in real arithmetic without retraining. Shared-context attention complements this output path by reusing prompt key/value blocks across beams while preserving their private decode tails. We implement both mechanisms in SGLang and evaluate candidate sourcing for LinkedIn Hiring Assistant and qualification retrieval for the Qualification Retrieval Platform. The combined system improves closed-loop throughput by up to 5.57x over the CLP baseline and up to 2.63x over BF16 FlashRec at a common beam width of 200 on the Qualification Retrieval Platform workload.

Breaking: Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

📅 10 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui.
  • Workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes.
  • It has been revealed that you can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

It has been revealed that you can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

In a recent development, all the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

Sources indicate that this is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

It has been revealed that in Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

It has been revealed that that same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

Recent findings suggest that there's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

In a recent development, this is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

In a recent development, the drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

This is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

Industry observers note that background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

It has been revealed that canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

Industry observers note that there are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

Sources indicate that AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

The image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

So far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

Recent findings suggest that A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:.

Industry observers note that zeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

This isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

Sources indicate that every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

The same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node highlights up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:.

Now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

Recent findings suggest that AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:.

bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

In a recent development, if you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

Recent findings suggest that whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

Really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes.

Analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arva AI, a company that deploys AI agents to make critical banking decisions, has secured $20m in Series A funding as it looks to push its accuracy-focused technology deeper into the bank back office.

Arthur Ventures led the round, and existing backers Y Combinator and Gradient also took part.

It has been revealed that according to the company, most back-office decisions at banks are still made manually, but this has begun to shift. Over the past year, Arva’s customers started entrusting notable decisions to its agents, with staff setting policies and monitoring outcomes.

During that period the firm rolled out its technology at scale with banks and FinTechs, among them a top-10 US bank, a payments institution listed on the S&P 500 and the global FinTech Wise.

In a recent development, arva argues that accuracy is the deciding factor in how much work a bank can delegate to AI. Areas such as financial crime compliance, onboarding, payment operations and lending generate a constant stream of decisions, most of which are still reviewed individually as backlogs grow. For AI to take on this work, banks must be able to trust each result and justify it to regulators. The company says general-purpose models fall short on both counts, lacking the required precision and often being unable to explain their reasoning.

In a recent development, arva’s agents manage critical decisions from beginning to end across compliance, onboarding, payments and lending. The company believes high accuracy depends on its models, agents and learning systems operating in tandem.

In September it set up Arva Research, an in-house lab developing proprietary models for the most accuracy-sensitive stages of a decision. Its agents draw on these models to process each case, while AgentCore, the firm’s continual learning infrastructure, tailors them to a given bank’s operations and policies over time.

Arva Intel, the lab’s debut model, carries out in-depth online research into individuals and businesses, and beat leading general-purpose models on accuracy by 13% in the organization’s testing.

Recent findings suggest that the fresh capital will support Arva Research’s development of further models and the expansion of AgentCore. Arva also intends to extend its agents to additional decision types, such as disputes, payment operations and lending.

This IDC Market Note contains an analysis on how Cameyo by Google, a virtual app delivery (VAD) solution, helps organizations deliver any legacy application over the web.

Organizations are increasingly adopting generative and agentic AI as they look for ways to unlock more business value. Yet for many IT leaders, business-critical legacy desktop apps stand in the way—too essential to retire, too complex and costly to rewrite—yet unequipped for the security challenges and productivity opportunities of the AI era.

It has been revealed that that doesn’t have to block your modernization strategy. By delivering Windows and legacy applications directly inside the Chrome browser, Cameyo by Google connects legacy workflows to Chrome Enterprise, ChromeOS, and Gemini—with zero replatforming required.

Sources indicate that in a recent IDC Market Note, “Cameyo by Google: A Modern Bridge Technology Platform in Digital Workspace Transformation,” lead analyst Filippo Vanara examines how Cameyo reduces deployment complexity while enhancing security and lowering costs. Here are five of our key takeaways from the IDC Market Note:.

In a recent development, enterprise modernization barriers make rewriting or replatforming legacy applications unfeasible for many organizations. The IDC report notes that "Cameyo is positioned as a strategic bridge between legacy application environments and modern, AI-driven digital workspaces." By connecting legacy systems to modern, AI-enhanced digital workspaces, Cameyo enables organizations to safeguard their existing technology investments.

Recent findings suggest that 2. Instant AI and security upgrades with Gemini and Chrome Enterprise.

In a recent development, moving legacy apps into the browser immediately surrounds them with modern capabilities they were never built to support. With Cameyo, legacy workflows run right alongside built-in enterprise AI like Gemini in Chrome—giving employees safe, managed AI tools instead of pushing them toward unmanaged "shadow AI." At the same time, apps can inherit Chrome’s advanced threat protections and Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies through Chrome Enterprise Premium, which the IDC Market Note highlights "This enables organizations to extend AI capabilities and modern security controls to legacy workflows.".

3. Protecting your organizations from cyberattacks.

Traditional VDI utilizes open VPNs and public server ports that leave organizations vulnerable to cyberattacks. According to the IDC Market Note, "As part of its value proposition, security is central to Cameyo. In fact, the platform adopts a zero trust architecture, isolating customers, sessions, and resources from the corporate network.” Additionally, "the use of non-persistent infrastructure and a simplified architecture reduces the overall attack surface.".

Industry observers note that 4. Slashing operational and virtualization costs.

According to IDC's 2025 EMEA CloudOps Survey (n = 509) findings, 89% of organizations in Europe estimated that they are currently wasting their public cloud spending. When companies use Cameyo as opposed to complex virtual desktops, they consistently realize reduced costs. According to the IDC Market Note, "Cost is another core value proposition for Cameyo as it emphasizes its potential to deliver significant cost savings compared with traditional VDI and DaaS solutions: up to 54% reduction in total cost of ownership (TCO) when transitioning from legacy environments.".

It has been revealed that 5. Phased modernization across endpoints.

According to the IDC Market Note, IDC believes Cameyo represents an crucial evolution within the broader VCC market, specifically reflecting a shift from desktop-centric virtualization to application-centric delivery models. In this context, the platform functions as a bridge technology, enabling enterprises to modernize incrementally rather than requiring full application replatforming. This aligns with IDC's view that most organizations will pursue phased modernization strategies, maintaining legacy software while gradually transitioning to cloud-native architectures.” By delivering legacy applications as Progressive Web Apps (PWAs), Cameyo helps businesses modernize without being tethered to a specific device or operating system. When paired with ChromeOS Flex, Cameyo can ensure seamless access to those legacy apps on older devices, extending existing hardware lifespans and reducing capital expenditures.

Industry observers note that adopting AI doesn't mean leaving legacy applications stranded. True workplace modernization integrates existing, business-critical software into a secure, unified AI ecosystem—without requiring complex app rewrites or costly migrations.

Tech Report: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams announces queues to simplify and reduce costs of real-time processing

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (302 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that amazon Kinesis Data Streams now supports queues, a simpler and more cost-effective way to process a stream.
  • Industry observers note that queues in Kinesis Data Streams are powered by Amazon SQS.
  • Use queues for applications that process each record independently, such as log processing, order fulfillment, and notifications.

Recent findings suggest that amazon Kinesis Data Streams now supports queues, a simpler and more cost-effective way to process a stream. Because queues track the delivery state of each record, your consumer instances receive records instead of leasing shards, acknowledge each record when processing is complete, and scale beyond the number of shards. Kinesis Data Streams consumers can reduce the cost of processing data by up to 43% by using queues instead of the Kinesis Client Library. You no longer run a DynamoDB table or custom metrics, and you use compute more efficiently.

Industry observers note that queues in Kinesis Data Streams are powered by Amazon SQS. Built on that foundation, a queue delivers records at least once, redelivers records your consumers do not acknowledge, and provides built-in dead-letter handling for records that keep failing. Each queue publishes its own CloudWatch metrics, so you can scale consumer instances on records waiting to be received and alarm on records that repeatedly fail.

Use queues for applications that process each record independently, such as log processing, order fulfillment, and notifications. Use a stream consumer when processing one record depends on the records before it, such as live analytics, personalization, and anomaly detection. You ingest data once and let each application consume records through a queue or directly from the stream, with no change to your producers or existing stream consumers. For point-to-point messaging between application components, start with Amazon SQS. Choose queues in Kinesis Data Streams when the same records are needed by multiple applications.

Queues are available for data streams in On-demand capacity mode. For regional availability, see Supported AWS Regions. To get started, see the developer guide, install the Kinesis Data Streams skill from the Agent Toolkit for AWS, read the launch blog, and see the pricing page.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.22307v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Editing a building information model in the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) schema requires propagating changes to dependent elements while preserving unrelated entities. Existing language-model agents for IFC editing use prompted models without learning from edit outcomes. Target-file comparisons do not specify which alternative edits are allowed or which unrelated entities must remain unchanged. We present IfcGym, a CodeAct environment in which a language model edits IFC through executable code and four checkers verify validity relative to the input model, intent, dependency and preservation against a task specification. Their conjunction is strict success. IfcEdit distils verified teacher episodes into a Qwen3.5-9B student through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), then applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with strict success as the reward. On IfcEditBench, 1,990 editing tasks on 13 held-out real projects, the final student reaches 86.78% strict success, from 79.15% after SFT. The paired confidence interval for the difference from its teacher includes zero; the same recipe on a 27B model reaches 91.76% and exceeds the teacher. On the public benchmarks BIM-Edit and BIBIMBAP the final student scores 55.19 and 54.50. On IfcEditBench, the students outperform all prompted models except the teacher under matched tool access; both evaluated frameworks also score lower. Rewarding all four checkers yields 4.83 points more strict success than rewarding intent and validity alone.
