Async GRPO with LoRA across HF Jobs: a bucket, a proxy, and no NCCL

📅 10 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that loRA support recently landed in TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer with PR #7017, and ships with TRL v1.14.
  • Sources indicate that loRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret.
  • There is also a systems consequence of LoRA training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that loRA support recently landed in TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer with PR #7017, and ships with TRL v1.14. The asynchronous trainer can now train an adapter instead of the full model, and it syncs only the LoRA adapter to vLLM. This post covers a real-world project built on top of it, where training and inference no longer share a machine.

Sources indicate that loRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret. They show that LoRA can match full fine-tuning for policy-gradient RL, even with rank 1. This stems from the fact that the advantage function only gives ~O(1) bits of information per episode, so there is not that much to learn from each step, from a total-bits-of-information point of view. A rank-1 adapter has enough capacity to absorb it.

There is also a systems consequence of LoRA training. A rank-1 adapter for a 1.5B model is a few megabytes, while the full model is around 3 GB. Instead of sending the full policy to the inference workers after every update, we can just send the adapter. vLLM can also keep several adapters loaded at once. Old rollouts finish with the policy they started with, while new rollouts use the latest one.

TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer already separates training and generation. The trainer and vLLM can run on different machines and at their own speed. This is easy in a single-node or cluster setting where both processes share a filesystem or can form an NCCL group.

It has been revealed that what we want is to run the same setup with Hugging Face Jobs. Essentially, an HF Job is one container running on one VM. This means that one Job cannot spawn multiple nodes (at least for now) to hold a trainer and a fleet of vLLM servers (we are limited to 8xH200 at most per node). The AsyncGRPOTrainer is built for exactly that kind of scale, so the question became: how far can we get if we drop the requirement that the trainer and the inference servers share a node?

According to recent reports, well, with a full-weight sync, the answer would be "not far". Every upgrade would have to move gigabytes between machines, which is what NCCL is for in a dense cluster, but Jobs can't communicate across nodes. There is no shared local disk and obviously no shared localhost. With LoRA, a sync is only a few megabytes. For the filesystem part, HF Jobs provide volumes backed by Storage Buckets! These buckets can then be mounted as a FUSE filesystem in every Job and are enough to work as a shared FS between nodes. No network path between the Jobs is needed at all.

The setup ended up being quite small:.

Recent findings suggest that the new adapter-only sync path in AsyncGRPOTrainer works like this. The trainer does not send tensors to vLLM. Every few optimizer steps, it saves the adapter under /.vllm_lora/trl-policy-v{N}, publishes the directory with an atomic rename, then sends its path to vLLM's /v1/load_lora_adapter endpoint. vLLM loads the files from disk, so the rollout worker can then request model="trl-policy-v{N}".

It has been revealed that this is how runtime adapter loading already works in vLLM. The endpoint takes a path, not tensors, so the trainer and the server are expected to share a filesystem. On a Slurm cluster, that is the network filesystem. On Jobs, we get the same thing by mounting a Storage Bucket as a volume at the same path in every Job, as we mentioned earlier. Under the hood, it uses hf-mount, which exposes the bucket as a POSIX filesystem inside the container:.

According to recent reports, nothing in TRL or vLLM had to change for this. The trainer writes to /lora//.vllm_lora/ and the servers read from the same path. The path sent in the POST request is already valid inside every container.

It has been revealed that note that we also store the checkpoints and the final adapter in the bucket. The HF Jobs are ephemeral, but a preempted trainer can resume training, as the final adapter is always persisted to the bucket and is never lost when the Job stops.

Recent findings suggest that each replica uses one GPU and the stock vllm/vllm-openai image. We only need to enable runtime LoRA loading and reserve enough adapter slots.

The number of adapter slots follows from max_staleness. In AsyncGRPOTrainer, every weight sync bumps the policy version by one, and max_staleness is how many versions a rollout sample may lag behind the current policy before the trainer discards it. With max_staleness=4, a sample generated under trl-policy-v3 is still used for training while the trainer is at v7. A rollout that started under v3 must also be able to finish under v3. So at any moment, vLLM has to serve the current policy plus the four before it. That is why the trainer keeps max_staleness + 1 adapter versions registered and unloads anything older. Each sync loads the fresh version before it unloads the oldest one, which needs one more slot during the swap. That gives --max-loras 6. With only five, vLLM would silently evict a policy that still has rollouts in flight at every sync.

Industry observers note that we pin vLLM to v0.27.1. vLLM moves fast, and the flags above and the runtime LoRA endpoints are the ones that version exposes, so treat the version as part of the recipe.

There is another possible design where the trainer keeps only the latest adapter and always publishes it under the same name. We did not go that way, because vLLM keys its prefix cache by adapter name. With a single name, KV blocks computed under the previous weights would still match after the swap, so the prefill would not be redone and a rollout could get its prefix from one policy version and its decode from the next. The trainer would have no way to tell, and it would show up as ratio drifting away from 1. Versioned names make this impossible: a name always means one set of weights, and a cached prefix can never match a newer version.

It has been revealed that we chose sail/Sanity-Test-R1D-1.5B, the dataset from Defeating the Training-Inference Mismatch via FP16 (Qi et al., 2025). The reproduction code is in sail-sg/Precision-RL.

The authors generated 40 answers for each MATH problem with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B. They kept problems with a success rate between 20% and 80%, yielding 1,460 questions. This dataset is really good for RL validation because the questions are neither already solved nor completely hopeless for that model, meaning the model can get a good early signal to train on and improve.

It has been revealed that this is awesome as a robust end-to-end test: if one vLLM replica silently serves the base model under an adapter name, we want to see that in the curve within a few dozen steps. Also, this dataset is small enough to cycle through in less than two hours.

We also take the hyperparameters from the paper's LoRA scripts in oat/scripts/lora: Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, LoRA rank 1 with alpha 2, a learning rate of 4e-5, 8 samples per prompt, 128 completions per step, a maximum of 3,000 generated tokens and a 4,096-token context.

The trainer uses the same vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1 image with TRL installed on top. We ran the PR branch at the time; the same code now ships in TRL v1.14. The training script is a normal AsyncGRPOTrainer script. The only Job-specific values are the output directory and the server URL.

According to recent reports, during initialization, TRL calls /server_info. If it finds a lora_config, it uses adapter-only sync. Configurations vLLM cannot serve directly, such as DoRA, modules_to_save, or a rank above --max-lora-rank, fall back to merged-weight sync with a warning. The log should contain Adapter-only vLLM sync enabled.

Now onto the fun stuff. We need a proxy between the trainer and the vLLM Jobs for two reasons:.

Exposed Job ports require an Authorization: Bearer header on every request. The proxy is where that header gets added, so TRL does not need to know about it.

We want more than one GPU generating. On a single vLLM server, the usual way to get that is --data-parallel-size > 1, but TRL refuses adapter-only sync in that mode, for a good reason: a call to /v1/load_lora_adapter only reaches the DP rank that answers it, so the other ranks would keep serving the base model under the upcoming policy name. On Jobs the question does not even arise, since each replica is its own machine. So the data parallelism has to live one level up, in something that fans the adapter load out to every replica.

We therefore run a small proxy at 127.0.0.1:8000 on the trainer Job and point TRL to it as if it were a single vLLM server. Besides adding the header, the proxy does two things functionally:.

A quick reminder of why this matters. Generating a completion has two phases with very different workload profiles:.

It has been revealed that those keys and values are the KV cache. Because attention is causal, the KV of a token depends only on the tokens before it, not on what comes after. Two requests that share a prefix therefore share the KV of that prefix, and a replica that already has it in cache can skip that part of the prefill entirely. The whole game now is to find that replica, so a request can benefit from landing on the replica that has already seen its prefix.

vLLM stores its prefix KV cache in blocks of 16 tokens. Because of GRPO, the rollout worker sends G requests with the same prompt (in our case G=8). If they all reach the same replica, the first request computes the prefill and the next seven reuse it. With round-robin routing, half would go to a replica that doesn't have the prefix cached, and those four requests would redo the prefill work and waste valuable GPU compute.

The job of our router is to track which replica has seen which block hash. One notable detail is that the hashes are chained, so the hash of block 3 represents blocks 1, 2 and 3, not just block 3. This mirrors causal attention: the KV of block 3 is only valid if blocks 1 and 2 are the same too. We also seed the chain with the adapter name because the KV cache also depends on the adapter that generated it: a prefix cached for policy v3 is useless for policy v4!

The video walks through the entire decision process for choosing a replica. The steps below go through a real 135-token completion request example (from the Sanity dataset problems):.

1. Split the prompt into blocks. The router receives token ids and cuts them into 16-token blocks, just like vLLM. It only hashes complete blocks, so the last 7 tokens are ignored here.

Sources indicate that 2. Hash the prefix. Each block is hashed with the previous hash, starting from the adapter seed. h3 therefore identifies blocks 1, 2 and 3 in order. Two prompts with the same first k blocks get the same hashes up to hk. Once one block changes, every hash after it changes too. This is why we seed the hashes with the adapter name: the same prompt under trl-policy-v4 starts from another seed and cannot match entries from v3. This is what we want because the old KV blocks were computed with different weights.

It has been revealed that 3. Compare two prompts. Problem 1 has 103 tokens. Both prompts start with the same 23-token chat template. Their first block is identical, but block 2 already contains the problem text. The hashes differ from there.

In a recent development, 4. Store the owners. For every hash, the router remembers which replicas served it and which hashes came after it (we cap the successor set at two because we only need to know whether a block has one continuation or several). After a few prompts, the template block h1 is owned by both replicas and already has several successors, h2 to h8 are owned by A only and each has a single successor, and h2' to h6' are owned by B only.

It has been revealed that in practice, every prompt in a run starts with the same tokens. Here, it is the chat template and the system prompt, which amount to the first 23 tokens of all 1,460 problems. In an agent setting, it would be the tool descriptions, and in a multi-turn environment it would be the shared conversation history. These blocks are in every replica's cache within seconds, so matching on them tells us nothing about where a particular prompt lives.

In a recent development, A block is common if every replica has served it, or if it has more than one successor. Common blocks are ignored during routing because they do not identify a particular prompt. More on this below!

5. Pick a replica. The router counts how many leading blocks match on each replica and removes the common prefix. What is left is the number of blocks specific to this prompt. Then:.

Here is the rule applied to four requests. Start from a state where replicas A and B both have 3 requests in flight, and only the template block h1 is known on both replicas.

6. Reuse the prefill. Request 2 is the reason for doing all this. It reuses the prefill computed by Request 1: blocks 1 to 8 are already in A's KV cache, so A skips straight to decoding the completion. Had it gone to B, B would have prefilled all 135 tokens again while A's cache sat unused. Request 3 shows why the common rule is needed. Without it, the shared chat template would make every newly introduced prompt look like a cache hit. Request 4 keeps the load bounded. Saving one prefill is not worth letting a replica fall far behind.

According to recent reports, the common prefix is the annoying part. Every request starts with the same system prompt and chat template. A simple longest-prefix match would give the first replica a match for almost every upcoming prompt. We detect the shared prefix through fan-out instead: a block with several different successors is common, while a block that always leads to the same successor belongs to a particular prompt. Only the blocks after that common prefix count as affinity.

In a recent development, the proxy also needs to broadcast the adapter loads to every replica. We treat the operation as all-or-nothing. Each replica has its own bucket mount, so they do not necessarily see a latest adapter at exactly the same time. A No adapter found for error usually means that one bucket mount has not caught up yet, and we retry only that replica. For any other error, we unload the adapter from the replicas that accepted it so that a policy name never exists on only part of the replicas.

We also broadcast /pause, /resume and /v1/unload_lora_adapter in the same way. /health returns 200 only if every replica is healthy. /server_info and /v1/models only need one answer. From TRL's point of view, the proxy is a single data_parallel_size=1 server, so it selects adapter-only sync.

According to recent reports, we initially wondered whether a Python asyncio proxy would become a bottleneck. It does not (at least at this scale). There are at most 128 non-streaming JSON requests in flight, and routing only computes a few hashes. One thread handles this easily. A more refined router that needs to handle more traffic would probably need to be written in a faster language (We see you 🦀).

Recent findings suggest that the numbers below come from the trainer's logged metrics on trackio. The run uses Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, LoRA r=1 on all-linear, 128 completions per step and 8 rollouts per prompt. It runs for 500 steps and saves a checkpoint every 50 steps. The trainer uses an h200x2 Job and each of the two vLLM replicas uses one h200 Job. Running all three costs ~$20 per hour.

All 252 adapter loads succeeded 🎉: 126 syncs times 2 replicas. Six succeeded on the second attempt and 246 on the third.

At the end of the run, after 64,728 rollouts, the proxy's counters read:.

With 8 rollouts per prompt, at least one of the eight requests must be cold. The theoretical minimum is therefore 12.5 %. The router gets 14.2 % unmatched requests, 84.5 % affinity hits, and 1.3 % spills. There is not much left to gain here unless we start looking at each replica's load using deeper inference-side metrics based on real measured load.

The first configuration has a pretty obvious problem: the trainer is the bottleneck, not generation. Over the 500 steps, we have:.

Sources indicate that the rollout queue stays full, and the worker is mostly blocked by backpressure. The second replica is basically useless in this configuration. We'll see later in the post how we went through runs that moved the bottleneck between training and generation to make the run 3.9× faster.

Figure 1. trackio run r1-dp2. Panels: reward with its 20-step rolling mean and 50-step block means, and ratio on a 0.99 to 1.01 axis. Reward climbs from 0.15 to 0.44 over 500 steps; ratio stays between 0.9993 and 1.0004 throughout.

Industry observers note that 500 steps took 3 h 27 min. Mean reward goes from 0.145 over the first 20 steps to 0.438 over the last 20. More importantly for this test, ratio stays at 1.000 for every step! The policy served by vLLM always matches the one used by the trainer to score the rollout. This held across all 126 syncs. Mean staleness was 1.5 policy versions, against a maximum of 4. The trackio dashboard has the full curves.

Industry observers note that we have our undeniable proof that LoRA AsyncGRPO works! Let's now see how we can improve our training runs by looking at the recent detailed AsyncGRPO metrics.

According to recent reports, async RL is a pipeline between training and generation. Making one side faster does nothing if the other side cannot keep up. Fortunately, in AsyncGRPOTrainer we've added enough timings and metrics to see this directly.

According to recent reports, all the useful metrics are documented in the Logged metrics section. perf/rollout_wait_s tells us how long the trainer waits for samples. rollout/backpressure_s tells us how long generation waits for space in the rollout queue. They are diametrically opposed to each other and should not both be high. Together with the queue size, they tell us which side is slow.

It has been revealed that we ran five experiments. Each one starts from a problem visible in the previous run's dashboard. Unless mentioned otherwise, the model, recipe and three-Job layout stay the same. The names below are the trackio run names.

We keep these four groups of metrics visible:.

In a recent development, the diagnosis is simple: a full queue with zero rollout wait and high backpressure means the trainer is too slow. An empty queue with rising rollout wait and no backpressure means generation is too slow. Comparing perf/mfu_wall_clock with perf/mfu_fwd_bwd also indicates how much time the trainer GPUs spend waiting instead of training.

Sources indicate that figure 2. trackio run r1-dp2. Panels: perf/step_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, sample/rollout_queue_size, rollout/backpressure_s. Step time and forward+backward overlap almost completely; the queue sits pinned near 476 of 512 and backpressure never drops below 11 s per rollout group: trainer-bound.

In a recent development, perf/step_s is 22.9 s and perf/fwd_bwd_s is 21.9 s. Forward and backward take 96 % of the step time. The queue stays full and the trainer waits only 0.02 s for rollouts, and the rollout worker spends 15 seconds per group blocked by backpressure. The two vLLM replicas generate faster than the trainer consumes. The reported 4.6k tokens/s is not their actual limit; they simply have nowhere to put more output.

It has been revealed that the batch metrics explain the terrible 3.9 % MFU. batch/microbatches_per_step is 64 and batch/samples_per_row is 1.0. Each rank processes one sequence of around 1.2k tokens, 64 times per step. This comes from the reference recipe's per_device_train_batch_size=1. For a 1.5B model on an H200, this is completely latency-bound.

Sources indicate that the fix is not to change the batch size. We keep 128 completions per optimizer step and only change how they are laid out on the GPU: instead of one sequence per microbatch, we pack many sequences densely into each row. The trainer supports this through token-budget batching. With token_budget > 0, it packs several samples into one padding-free row per rank. An optimizer step processes gradient_accumulation_steps rows. We set token_budget=16384 and gradient_accumulation_steps=6.

Industry observers note that figure 3. trackio runs r1-dp2 and r1-dp2-tb16k overlaid over their first 154 steps. Panels: batch/samples_per_row, batch/microbatches_per_step, perf/step_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, perf/mfu_fwd_bwd, rollout/generated_tok_s. Packing takes samples per row from 1 to 13, microbatches from 64 to 6, step time from 23 s to 5.9 s, and generation from 4.2k to 27.5k tok/s with no change on the vLLM side.

batch/samples_per_row goes from 1.0 to ~12.7 and the number of microbatches drops from 64 to 6. The rows are 95 % full! Forward and backward fall from 21.9 s to 5.6 s, while MFU rises from 3.9 % to 19 %. We now train on around 150 samples per step because the rows pack better than the mean-length estimate predicted.

Generation also jumps from 4.6k to 25k tokens/s, even though we changed nothing on the vLLM side. The queue is no longer constantly full, so the replicas can finally run. This is why we do not like optimizing pipeline stages in isolation. We need to be careful to evaluate the whole system, as a slow stage can hide the real performance of everything before it.

Recent findings suggest that perf/fwd_s is 1.34 s while perf/fwd_bwd_s is 5.6 s. A normal backward costs roughly twice the forward, and with frozen base weights it should be closer to once. A ratio of 3.2 is suspicious.

According to recent reports, the reason is that AsyncGRPOConfig defaults to gradient_checkpointing=True. Every microbatch recomputes its forward during the backward. This also explains why a 16k-token row only uses 25 GB on a 141 GB H200! It's a memory optimization for this trainer, but we don't need it in this specific case: the model is small enough to fit into VRAM with the activations kept for the backward.

It has been revealed that figure 4. trackio runs r1-dp2-tb16k and r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt overlaid over their first 134 steps. Panels: perf/fwd_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, perf/weight_sync_s, sample/rollout_queue_size, perf/rollout_wait_s, perf/mfu_fwd_bwd. Forward+backward drops by one forward; the queue falls from ~420 to ~60, and rollout wait rises from 0.02 s to 0.5 s: the bottleneck shifts to generation.

In a recent development, with gradient_checkpointing=False, forward and backward drop to 4.6 s, almost exactly one forward less, and MFU reaches 23 %. The queue now falls to 71 and rollout wait rises from 0.04 s to 0.6 s. The trainer consumes samples faster than two replicas generate them. We successfully moved the bottleneck to generation.

This exposes two more costs. A 7.6-second weight sync every four steps now takes 25 % of wall-clock time. It was only 8 % when each step took 23 seconds. Also, backward is still 2.5 times slower than forward. With frozen base weights, there are around 2 seconds per step that do not look like normal model math.

Since generation was now too slow, we added a third replica. We also reduced the adapter retry interval from 2 s to 0.5 s in the proxy and disabled fsdp_reshard_after_forward to check whether FSDP2 re-gathers caused the extra 2 seconds in backward.

Figure 5. trackio runs r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt and r1-dp3-tb16k-nockpt overlaid over their first 134 steps. Panels: perf/weight_sync_s, rollout/generated_tok_s, rollout/inflight, perf/fwd_bwd_s. Sync falls from 7.6 s to 5.8 s; generation and forward+backward do not move; rollout/inflight reads 128 in both runs, which is the cap the third replica ran into.

In a recent development, weight sync falls from 7.6 s to 5.8 s, so the shorter retry helps. Forward and backward stay at 4.6 s, which rules out resharding. Generation moves from 25k to only 26k tokens/s. The third replica does basically nothing.

Sources indicate that the reason was sitting in rollout/inflight: 128 in every run. The proxy shows those requests split as 44 + 43 + 41 across the three replicas. max_inflight_tasks limits concurrency for the whole rollout worker, not per replica. A 1.5B model on an H200 processes 43 and 130 concurrent sequences at almost the same cost per token. Splitting 128 requests over three GPUs gives nearly the same throughput as splitting them over two.

Sources indicate that so vLLM was not the limit. Our own client-side constant was. We had set it conservatively because we did not know how hundreds of long HTTPS requests would behave through the public Jobs proxy. At this point, 130,000 rollout completions had crossed it without a single transport error.

max_inflight_tasks=384 and queue_maxsize=768, nothing else.

It has been revealed that figure 6. All five trackio runs (r1-dp2, r1-dp2-tb16k, r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt, r1-dp3-tb16k-nockpt, r1-dp3-inflight384) overlaid, x-axis in steps. Panels: perf/step_s, reward, sample/rollout_queue_size, sample/staleness_mean. Step time falls from 22.9 s to 4.8 s across the series while the reward curves stay on top of each other; the last run's queue refills to ~690 of 768 and its staleness settles at 2. Runs 2 to 4 were stopped early once the dashboard had answered the question.

It has been revealed that with 384 requests in flight, each replica gets 128. The queue quickly fills to around 690 out of 768 and stays there. Backpressure returns to 5 seconds and rollout wait falls to 0.03 seconds. Training is the bottleneck again! Forward and backward take 4.6 seconds, weight sync adds an amortized 1.5 seconds, and median step time is 4.8 seconds.

Recent findings suggest that mean staleness rises from 1.5 to 2.0 versions because samples wait longer in the larger queue. This is still below max_staleness=4, and ratio remains very close to 1.000.

Figure 7. trackio runs r1-dp2 and r1-dp3-inflight384, reward against wall-clock minutes since the first optimizer step. Same recipe, same 500 steps, same final reward; run 5 gets there in 52 minutes instead of 3 h 26 min.

According to recent reports, the final run is 3.9× faster and trains on 31 % more samples, with basically the same reward curve. Packing, disabling checkpointing and raising the in-flight limit made the difference. In each case, the dashboard made this clear within the first ten minutes.

Recent findings suggest that loRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret. They show that LoRA can match full fine-tuning for policy-gradient RL, even with sportzfy rank 1. This stems from the fact that the advantage function only gives ~O(1) bits of information per episode, so there is not that much to learn from each step, from a total-bits-of-information point of view. A rank-1 adapter has enough capacity to absorb it.

Really interesting take on how LoRA changes the systems side of RL training, not just the training itself. The idea of separating training and inference across different machines while only moving a small adapter instead of the full model makes a lot of practical sense, especially when working with HF Jobs. The “bucket, proxy, and no NCCL” approach feels like a good example of simplifying distributed infrastructure by moving the communication boundary to something much smaller and easier to manage.

In a recent development, I also like the connection to the LoRA Without Regret work, particularly the point that policy-gradient updates may not require huge adapter capacity to capture the useful signal. Sending only a few MB instead of several GB after updates can make a massive difference in both bandwidth and iteration speed. Would be really interested to see more details on how the bucket/proxy setup behaves at scale and whether there are any noticeable trade-offs once the number of inference workers or concurrent rollouts increases.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connect Money, an Egypt-based FinTech offering embedded finance and white-label card services, has secured $3.5m in a pre-Series A round as it gears up to take its platform into Saudi Arabia and Morocco.
  • The round was led by returning backers Mohamed Farouk, Algebra Ventures and DisrupTech Ventures, according to a report from Wamda.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connect Money, an Egypt-based FinTech offering embedded finance and white-label card services, has secured $3.5m in a pre-Series A round as it gears up to take its platform into Saudi Arabia and Morocco.

The round was led by returning backers Mohamed Farouk, Algebra Ventures and DisrupTech Ventures, according to a report from Wamda. The deal blends new funding with the sale of secondary shares, giving a number of the startup’s early backers a partial exit. Connect Money has not revealed what portion of the $3.5m is new capital.

The company will use the money to move into its two latest target markets, with obtaining regulatory sign-off and building the necessary infrastructure being the main priorities. In Saudi Arabia, the firm is pursuing a licence from the Saudi Central Bank (SAMA). In Morocco, it is putting in place local operations and technology systems, with a commercial launch pencilled in for the first half of 2027.

In a recent development, the move will take Connect Money’s embedded finance offering outside its home market for the first time. It is aimed at businesses that want to provide payment products to their customers but would rather not build banking infrastructure themselves.

Connect Money notes it has issued more than 300,000 cards so far. The platform aims to help businesses reach customers who rely on cash by giving them access to digital payments, instant lending tools and a network of more than 20,000 marketplace partners.

The firm takes care of the complicated parts of card issuance, so that companies can launch their own banking proposition through white-label cards paired with a digital banking app. Connect Money claims this lets clients skip long regulatory processes, large upfront spending and continuing operational costs. It also says businesses can open up fresh banking-related revenue streams without any initial investment.

MCTS Is Counting the Wrong Thing: Learning Exploration Counts for LLM Reasoning

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (205 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.22301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) has powered landmark successes in reinforcement learning, yet its gains in LLM reasoning can remain modest despite substantial search effort. We identify an overlooked bottleneck: what MCTS counts. Standard UCT assigns independent visit counts to textual branches, allowing different formulations of the same reasoning strategy to repeatedly receive exploration bonuses. Our theoretical analysis shows that this count fragmentation can impair exploration efficiency, as quantified by increased cumulative regret. To address this problem, we introduce Learned Pseudo-Count MCTS (LPC-MCTS), which changes only the exploration statistic in UCT. A lightweight Coin-Flipping Network head on the policy's hidden representations estimates representation coverage, enabling related branches to share exploration evidence. Across 5 mathematical-reasoning and 7 search benchmarks, LPC-MCTS consistently outperforms strong MCTS baselines. Holding each LPC-MCTS-trained policy fixed, replacing standard MCTS counts at inference improves average mean@16 accuracy across 5 mathematical benchmarks by 3.79 percentage points on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.71 points on Qwen3-4B. Applying LPC-MCTS during both training and inference yields gains of 4.96 and 4.37 points over standard MCTS, respectively. Together, our theory and experiments show that changing what MCTS counts can substantially improve its exploration efficiency and reasoning performance.

#10002. ARMORY CASTLE Exploits vSphere

ARMORY CASTLE Exploits vSphere

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3619 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stop attacks, reduce risk, and advance your security.
  • Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, John Palmisano, Steve Rasch, Daniel Sislo, John Wolfram.
  • 15, 2026, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published a blog post detailing recent activity in which the suspected PRC-nexus threat actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-102764, a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support, which was patched in BT26-05.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stop attacks, reduce risk, and advance your security.

Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, John Palmisano, Steve Rasch, Daniel Sislo, John Wolfram.

On Oct. 15, 2026, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published a blog post detailing recent activity in which the suspected PRC-nexus threat actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-102764, a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support, which was patched in BT26-05. We also described some of the threat actor’s post-exploitation operations. In this blog we describe additional post-compromise activity involving the exploitation of a vulnerability in VMware vCenter and the deployment of additional malware families.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 19, 2026, VMware disclosed CVE-2026-123890, which impacts VMware vCenter Server deployments. vSphere consists of both ESXi (the hypervisor) and vCenter Server. The vCenter server is a centralized platform deployed as a Photon Linux virtual appliance and is used to configure, control, and monitor ESXi host environments. CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC). Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local. Using the authenticated administrator session, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the data.mdb database, by leveraging the vCenter Server Directory Service (vmdird) RPC interface vmdirdbcp. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by Broadcom to remediate the vulnerability.

ARMORY CASTLE exploited this vulnerability in early September 2026 using BONESAW, according to forensic evidence. BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang , which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account.

In a recent development, ARMORY CASTLE’s use of BONESAW represents significant upcoming insight into this threat actor’s post-exploitation tactics. In this campaign, ARMORY CASTLE exploited two zero-days, and deployed three sets of malware specifically tailored for operating on targeted devices, indicating deep platform expertise and substantial resource backing. We are publishing this analysis, along with mitigation and hardening guidance, to support defenders in detecting this threat.

It has been revealed that moving laterally from the Remote SupportRemote Support device, ARMORY CASTLE established a foothold on an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and staged a suite of malware to support expanding access, persistence, and targeting of vCenter. ARMORY CASTLE exploited a zero-day vulnerability to gain access to the VMware server, and likely used an additional set of malware customized to this environment to conduct reconnaissance, credential theft, and data theft.

Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE lateral movement and vCenter compromise sequence of events.

Following the establishment of persistence and the deployment of lateral movement capabilities on the Remote Support appliance, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE conducting internal reconnaissance. This reconnaissance was heavily focused on VMware systems, based on the specific ports ARMORY CASTLE scanned and the URIs the group visited such as /sdk and /ui. The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012. Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of ARMORY CASTLE’s remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW.

Figure 2: ARMORY CASTLE nmap port scanning.

Recent findings suggest that ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to internal Linux appliances within the environment that lacked endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. ARMORY CASTLE deployed five newly identified malware families and utilities: the SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH webshells, the BEARBONES backdoor, the BONESAW remote exploitation utility, and the SAWSNAKE SAML utility. ARMORY CASTLE also deployed the LAZYBONES backdoor, which Mandiant and GTIG previously observed in a separate ARMORY CASTLE intrusion.

Industry observers note that to establish a foothold on the first Linux appliance, the actor dropped a webshell ActiveSer.jsp, tracked by Mandiant as SLIMSAVAGE. SLIMSAVAGE functions as an upgraded command execution webshell that utilizes the authentication secret pwd=123.

According to recent reports, by leveraging ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", ...), the SLIMSAVAGE webshell executed commands inside a command line interpreter, enabled shell pipelines, redirects, creation of environment variables, and chained execution. The webshell reads from both standard output (getInputStream()) and standard error (getErrorStream()), ensuring full diagnostic visibility. It also calls Process.waitFor() and appends the final process return code (\nEXIT:).

Roughly 4 hours later, ARMORY CASTLE deployed an additional webshell to the Linux appliance, u.jsp, tracked as CAGEMATCH. While SLIMSAVAGE provided the group with a robust capability to execute commands on the appliance, the group was limited in their ability to transfer data. To solve this challenge, CAGEMATCH acts as a dedicated payload staging webshell. The webshell checks for a multipart/form-data request header, parses the boundary delimiter, and extracts raw file bytes along with the original filename.

Figure 4: CAGEMATCH File Staging Logic.

CAGEMATCH creates the /tmp directory if necessary, saves the uploaded payload directly to /tmp/, and echoes the absolute target path back to the client. When accessed without an upload payload, it returns a minimal HTML upload form. This provides the attacker with a streamlined post-exploitation workflow: using CAGEMATCH to upload binary payloads, scripts, or tools from the Remote Support appliance directly into /tmp, and subsequently invoke SLIMSAVAGE to adjust execution permissions and execute the staged tools.

To escalate privileges to root on the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE repeated the same escalation technique used on the Remote Support appliance through the enablement of Set User ID (SUID) permissions on the binary /bin/env. ARMORY CASTLE performed this permission modification using the GNU Debugger, gdb. By enabling SUID permissions on the binary /bin/env, any user would be allowed to execute commands as root.

Figure 5: ARMORY CASTLE gdb Privilege Escalation.

In a recent development, after successfully escalating privileges to root, ARMORY CASTLE began staging additional tooling on the Linux appliance to enable lateral movement within the environment. ARMORY CASTLE used curl to download the RAR utility from the Remote Support appliance.

Figure 6: ARMORY CASTLE downloads staged RAR utility.

ARMORY CASTLE then utilized curl to download a rar archive 123.rar which was subsequently extracted using their downloaded RAR binary.

Figure 7: ARMORY CASTLE extracts BONESAW.

Industry observers note that tracked as BONESAW, /tmp/123 is a remote exploitation utility written in Golang that leverages CVE-2026-123890 in vCenter to enable remote arbitrary LMDB exfiltration, SAML STS hijacking, and SSO administrator account creation. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leveraging this utility to target an internal vCenter server, successfully creating an SSO admin account, exfiltrating and parsing the LMDB which enabled lateral movement to the server.

BONESAW achieves full system compromise against vCenter Server 7.x and 8.x appliances through the exploitation of CVE-2026-123890. This vulnerability exploits a cryptographic logic and authorization flaw in VMware's rpc_srp_verifier service over port 2012, exposing a shared session key that can be used to create authenticated sessions as administrator@vsphere.local. BONESAW also provides the ability to stream the raw underlying LMDB file for offline parsing, extract the VMware Security Token Service (STS) SAML private RSA signing key, create a backdoor machine account via vmdir, forge administrative SAML 2.0 assertion tokens, and assign Global Administrator privileges on the vCenter root folder via the vSphere SOAP API.

Recent findings suggest that while CVE-2026-123890 shares some overlap with CVE-2026-59309, primarily the obtaining of the shared session key "K" without knowing the password, there are multiple key differences between them. CVE-2026-59309 is a flaw in the vCenter Server vmdir daemon that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker with network access to TCP ports 389 or 636 to send crafted LDAP packets with malformed authorization tokens, bypassing authentication to forge administrative sessions and create rogue Single Sign-On (SSO) accounts in the vSphere directory. Whereas CVE-2026-123890 is a flaw in the vmdir DCE/RPC interface that enables unauthenticated Secure Remote Password session key disclosure by exploiting predictable UUIDv1 timestamp generation in the SRP authentication interface, enabling the compromise of the SRP session key without knowing any passwords.

Mandiant has evidence that ARMORY CASTLE had knowledge of CVE-2026-123890 prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026. Logs indicate that BONESAW was executed in early September 2026 against a vCenter server already patched against CVE-2026-59309, and the recovered Go binary contains a build timestamp of 2026-07-13T09:21:24Z (16 days before CVE-2026-59309 was disclosed), although Go build metadata can be modified prior to compilation.

Industry observers note that ARMORY CASTLE named BONESAW vcenter-db-teamcheck-go and compiled it in a Windows development environment based on Golang build artifacts: E:/CodeFiles/VulnScan/Vcenter/go_teamcheck/. BONESAW supports multiple command-line arguments, with primary functionality centered on the csa subcommand to remotely create an SSO admin account.

Figure 8: BONESAW Command Line Arguments.

When executed utilizing the CSA command line flag, BONESAW creates the following files on disk:.

Figure 9: BONESAW Filesystem Artifacts.

SAWSNAKE parses command-line arguments to determine its operating mode and supports the following command line arguments:.

Figure 10: SAWSNAKE Command Line Arguments.

SAWSNAKE creates the following files on disk:.

Figure 11: Files created by SAWSNAKE.

Recent findings suggest that mandiant identified a second sample of SAWSNAKE that is likely an updated version. This sample added verbose debug logging to standard output across TLS, HTTP, SAML initiation, XML signing, and login routines, along with expanded redirect handling for up to 10 HTTP 302 redirects to support multi-hop authentication. Consistent with earlier activity, ARMORY CASTLE deleted SAWSNAKE and its output files from disk using rm.

Recent findings suggest that shortly after the deployment of SAWSNAKE, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged an additional backdoor /tmp/dbr tracked as BEARBONES. BEARBONES is written in C and is based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server. It is capable of bypassing system password authentication when using password-based authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from /tmp instead of the default directory /etc/dropbear. The authentication handler svr_auth_password for the packet type SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST was backdoored to bypass /etc/shadow validation and grant access if the SHA-256 digest of the first 14 bytes of client password matches a hardcoded SHA-256 hash, while also logging plaintext credentials. Additionally, the internal version string and the session identification string were modified to “23345” and “SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345”. Pivoting on this SSH banner identified a suspected obfuscation network of compromised third-party firewalls and routers exposing SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345 on non-standard high TCP ports.

ARMORY CASTLE executed BEARBONES several times from the Linux appliance, first attempting to open a listener on TCP port 53 and later on TCP port 33992.

Figure 12: BEARBONES Command Line Execution.

Sources indicate that after the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named sps-@vsphere.local. Notably, ARMORY CASTLE enabled SSH on vCenter via the vCenter Server Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) API through a PUT request to /rest/appliance/access/ssh. Mandiant also observed this TTP during BRICKSTORM intrusions conducted by suspected PRC-nexus actor UNC6201. After enabling SSH, ARMORY CASTLE connected to the vCenter via SSH using the newly created local administrator account.

Recent findings suggest that ARMORY CASTLE then conducted credential theft, targeting the vCenter internal master crypto key file as well as the PostgreSQL password file using SSH. ARMORY CASTLE disabled the SSH service via the VAMI API immediately after extracting the vCenter master symmetric key and PostgreSQL database credentials. ARMORY CASTLE then was observed authenticating to ESXi Host Client (“ESXUI”) using the vpxuser account and also connected to it via SSH using the root account.

Industry observers note that ARMORY CASTLE used the WinSCP client to enumerate the ESXi file system, attached disks, mounted Virtual Machine File System (VMFS) volumes, and added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys. ARMORY CASTLE conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account. The actor was primarily observed enumerating directories and VMFS volumes. To stage and exfiltrate data from the ESXi filesystem, ARMORY CASTLE created a hidden directory, .a, on a VMFS volume to which they established an SCP connection to the ESXi using scp -r -d -t "/vmfs/volumes//.a". ARMORY CASTLE then staged and extracted a suspected VMware specific toolset onto the ESXi host using tar xzf vmfs-pydist.tar.gz.

Figure 13: ARMORY CASTLE reconnaissance of guest VMs.

ARMORY CASTLE then archived the extracted files into o.tar.gz, copied the archive from the ESXi filesystem using scp -r -p -d -f "o.tar.gz", and deleted the hidden .a directory. On the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE staged the corresponding OpenSSH RSA private key at /tmp/123.key (matching the public key added to ESXi root authorized_keys) to authenticate outbound from the Linux appliance to ESXi over SSH without a password, alongside the BEARBONES SSH listener on the Linux appliance. From the Linux appliance, staged archives were downloaded via HTTP GET requests to the Remote Support appliance, from which ARMORY CASTLE likely exfiltrated the data.

Figure 14: ARMORY CASTLE SSH Tunnel.

Sources indicate that ARMORY CASTLE deployed a Slack-based backdoor tracked as LAZYBONES (/usr/bin/vmtoolscs) to an additional Linux appliance alongside the /tmp/123.key SSH private key. ARMORY CASTLE established persistence using a systemd service file set to restart every 50 minutes. LAZYBONES is a lightweight backdoor, written in Go, that establishes command-and-control (C2) communication over HTTPS using Slack. This malware periodically checks the most recent message in a designated Slack channel for commands. LAZYBONES supports core backdoor functionalities, including command execution and file transfer. Specifically, this variant encrypts Slack C2 messages with AES-256-CTR prior to Base64 encoding, polls with a 150 to 450 second jitter interval, and supports four commands (cmd, upload, download, and sleep) for command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE deploying LAZYBONES in a separate campaign in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of CVE-2025-22457.

GTIG attributes this activity to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). As noted in our prior blog, the tooling and TTPs leveraged within this campaign align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE, and in the case of LAZYBONES, directly overlap with previously observed activity.

In a recent development, while GTIG and Mandiant have tracked ARMORY CASTLE exploiting zero-days and n-days in edge and security appliances for initial access since 2023, BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days. The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and vmfs_browser.py, alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each. The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single compromise indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations. It also reveals the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets. Lastly, it is notable to highlight that the build time of BONESAW predates its deployment in this intrusion by over a month, indicating it was likely developed for broader operations.

Recent findings suggest that the exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 by ARMORY CASTLE underscores a reality: virtualization infrastructure such as VMware vCenter remains a prime target for advanced persistent threats (APTs). Because vCenter serves as the centralized control plane for the virtualized data center, relying solely on reactive patching is insufficient to protect it. Organizations must adopt a proactive, Zero Trust approach to infrastructure hardening to defend against current and undiscovered zero-day vulnerabilities.

For a comprehensive framework on securing virtualization platforms against advanced persistent threats, organizations are highly advised to consult the Mandiant guide  vSphere and BRICKSTORM Malware: A Defender's Guide. This guide details an infrastructure-centric defense strategy, encompassing STIG benchmarking, identity management via Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs), and transforming the vCenter appliance into a proactive security sensor.

To secure vulnerable systems, it is highly recommended that affected organizations promptly deploy the official Broadcom patch.

The Risks of Default Configurations: The VCSA Host-Based Firewall.

Industry observers note that A common misconception in defending the vCenter control plane is that the native VCSA host-based firewall managed via the Virtual Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) provides adequate protection against lateral movement. In practice, relying on this default GUI-based firewall introduces severe operational and security limitations that threat actors like ARMORY CASTLE exploit:.

Industry observers note that lack of Port-Specific Granularity: The native VAMI GUI lacks the precision required for a Zero Trust model. To grant an internal server (such as a backup server) legitimate access to the vSphere API on TCP 443, an administrator is often forced to trust that IP for all ports. If that internal server is compromised, the attacker inherits an unobstructed path to highly sensitive management interfaces like SSH (22) and the VAMI (5480).

Circular Administrative Dependency: The VCSA firewall is managed via the VAMI, which resides on TCP port 5480. If an attacker gains VAMI access as ARMORY CASTLE demonstrated to enable SSH,  they can use their compromised role to deactivate the firewall entirely.

Forensic Visibility Gaps: The VAMI firewall is designed for connectivity management, not security monitoring, and does not generate remote logs for denied connection attempts or shell activity. This blinds the SOC to active lateral movement and port scanning.

Inbound-Only Policy: The default GUI focuses exclusively on inbound traffic, leaving outbound (egress) policy unmanaged. This allows malware on a compromised VCSA to communicate freely with external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure.

Proactive Hardening with the VCSA Hardening Tool.

To secure the vCenter control plane against advanced campaigns and future zero-days, Mandiant recommends utilizing the VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool.

Industry observers note that this script bypasses the vulnerable VAMI GUI and enforces security configurations directly at the Photon Linux kernel level via iptables. By transitioning the appliance to a strict "Default Deny" posture, enforcing granular egress filtering, and bridging kernel-level events to a remote SIEM, the tool transforms the VCSA from a passive appliance into an active security sensor.

The table below illustrates how deploying this proactive hardening script would have disrupted ARMORY CASTLE's attack chain at multiple stages, demonstrating its efficacy against zero-day exploits.

Impact on the ARMORY CASTLE Attack Chain.

Protection Against Future Zero-Days.

VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy & Connection Logging (Management Ports).

The nmap scans targeting TCP ports 443, 5480, and 22 are silently dropped because the attacker's source IP is not in the trusted whitelists. These blocked connection attempts are instantly forwarded to the SIEM via the iptables-log-bridge.sh service, exposing the active network reconnaissance.

Conceals critical management interfaces from internal network mapping tools and provides high-fidelity, early-warning alerts of active lateral movement before exploitation can occur.

VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 443).

Provides defense-in-depth: Even if a zero-day allows credential theft or authentication bypass on a backend service, the stolen credentials/tokens cannot be used to access the management plane from an untrusted network.

VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 2010).

An iptables DROP policy on TCP 2012 for non-allowlisted IPs prevents the exploit payload originating from a compromised Linux appliance from reaching the vmdird service.

Drops unauthorized inbound connections to management interfaces and RPC services, mitigating network-level exploitation of vulnerable services.

VCSA iptables Inbound DROP Policy (TCP 22 & 5480).

Sources indicate that blocks the OS-level pivot. The firewall drops the PUT request to the VAMI API (TCP 5480 or 443) used to enable the SSH daemon. Furthermore, even if SSH was already enabled, the VCSA_SSH_RULES chain drops all SSH connections.

Protects the underlying OS and databases from direct credential theft or tampering. Even if an attacker gains administrative privileges within the web application, they are blocked from dropping down to a root shell.

VCSA iptables Egress DROP Policy.

An egress DROP policy prevents SCP data exfiltration and blocks the LAZYBONES backdoor from establishing HTTPS C2 communications with external Slack endpoints.

Blocks unauthorized outbound internet and internal network connections, preventing the VCSA from acting as a pivot point or establishing external C2.

VCSA OS-Level Command and Syslog Auditing.

Remote syslog forwarding captures the execution of tar and Python vmfs_browser.py over SSH, exposing the extraction of NTDS.dit and registry hives in real-time.

Forwards bash command execution and dropped network packets to a SIEM, bypassing local anti-forensics (e.g., .bash_history deletion) and alerting on unauthorized shell activity.

VCSA Kernel-Level Rule Enforcement.

iptables rules operate independently of the VAMI application, preventing the actor from using the VAMI API (/rest/appliance/access/ssh) to circumvent network security controls.

Decouples network security from the vCenter application layer, ensuring firewall policies cannot be modified via compromised VAMI or vSphere administrative credentials.

Table 1: VCSA Hardening Features.

Note: When implementing iptables-based rules, we strongly advise rigorous testing and formal change control processes prior to production implementation.

Industry News: Arcesium unveils Blue platform for growing hedge funds

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that blue pairs cloud-native software with premium managed services.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arcesium, a global technology provider serving the investment sector, has rolled out Arcesium Blue, an integrated, AI-ready platform that gives expanding hedge funds a complete front-to-back setup from the moment they go live.

Recent findings suggest that blue pairs cloud-native software with premium managed services. It is aimed at funds running long/short equity, macro, simple credit or single-strategy books. Its purpose is to spare managers from building complicated operational infrastructure themselves, so they can concentrate on generating returns while they grow.

Industry observers note that the platform covers real-time portfolio management, order and execution management, compliance and risk, and post-trade operations, linking each stage of the investment lifecycle in one connected system. Newly launched and rapidly expanding funds often run into disjointed technology and configuration problems. Blue tackles this with a unified stack backed by experienced, institutional-grade professionals who provide managed services.

It has been revealed that on the front-office side, portfolio managers can monitor P&L in real time, simulate trades and run stress tests. The order management system lets customers allocate across asset classes from a single order entry screen. Day-to-day tasks such as reporting, accounting, reconciliations and data management take place within the platform and are overseen by Arcesium’s operations specialists. Compliance and risk processes rely on tight data controls and a full audit trail, so firms work with verified data at every stage.

The Aquata data platform sits at the core of Blue. It offers ready-made connections to external parties and systems, sophisticated data management tools and support for AI-native workflows, which keeps the front office and operational systems aligned on a single set of figures. Owners also get full access to Arcesium Intelligence, an embedded AI environment that works with any model and includes hundreds of preconfigured agents and applications designed to speed up decision-making.

Because Blue uses a focused scope and standardised configurations, it can be deployed promptly through one provider. As funds mature and take on more sophisticated strategies, they can move into the broader Arcesium ecosystem for a tailored setup without rebuilding their systems.

Arcesium CEO Gaurav Suri remarked, “Hedge funds require confidence and trust in the technologies and services that fuel their daily operations. This peace of mind allows managers to focus on what they do best without the constraints of fragmented infrastructure. Blue enables funds to focus on growth, with a full front-to-back offering, AI-readiness, and seasoned experts who take investment operations off their plates.

“Clients can take an idea from order to allocation, and through the full trade lifecycle, in one workflow — all powered by AI for efficiency and insight.

DYNO, an Offenburg-based digital occupational pension provider, has joined forces with lemon.markets, a Berlin-based Brokerage-as-a-Service FinTech, to add Germany’s latest state-subsidised retirement investment account, the Altersvorsorgedepot (AVD), to its platform.

Recent findings suggest that starting in 2027, staff at the more than 650 businesses that currently use DYNO will be able to manage both an occupational pension (bAV) and an AVD in a single place. lemon.markets will run the brokerage and custody backbone for the AVD, handling everything from opening accounts and safekeeping assets to processing subsidies and tax.

It has been revealed that the move turns DYNO from a provider focused only on occupational pensions into a broader retirement platform. Until now it has offered ETF-based bAV contracts without commission, and the AVD extends its reach into private retirement saving. Its “Pension Intelligence” tool combines the statutory, occupational and private pension pillars in a single view, helping employees understand how to maximise employer contributions and government subsidies.

Through its integrated API platform, lemon.markets manages the full investment chain behind the AVD. As an investment firm licensed by BaFin, it supplies a compliant, off-the-shelf private retirement account, meaning DYNO does not need to build its own execution, custody, subsidy or tax functions.

DYNO retains ownership of its relationships with employers and staff and operates the customer-facing interface. For lemon.markets, the deal represents its first step into occupational pensions and opens up employers as a fresh distribution route.

According to recent reports, DYNO was set up in 2021 by Marc Karkossa and Luis Weber and applies the neobroker approach to workplace pensions. It describes itself as the first digital platform allowing firms and their staff to arrange commission-free, ETF-based pension contracts directly, which it indicates cuts costs, improves transparency and delivers stronger long-term returns.

lemon.markets gives banks, asset managers and FinTechs access to capital markets via a single API, works with firms such as Pleo, Holvi, Optio and Tomorrow, and has been part of the dwpbank Group since August 2025, which holds more than €2.4 trillion in assets under custody.

DYNO co-founder and CEO Marc Karkossa said, “Retirement saving tends to work best for people who already know their way around finance. Many employees would benefit from a good retirement product but never get one, simply because nobody guides them.

According to recent reports, “We built DYNO to change that. With the AVD, we now cover a second product and show each employee how to use both to get the most out of employer contributions and state subsidies.”.

lemon.markets founder and CEO Max Linden mentioned, “Whether someone gets a good occupational pension should not depend on union membership, a collective agreement or a works council. Most employees in small and mid-sized companies meet none of these conditions. Bringing bAV and AVD together on one platform makes retirement savings easier to manage. That is what DYNO is building for 2027, with lemon.markets as its infrastructure partner.”.

#9998. Breaking: Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

📅 15 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1833 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

📅 15 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1833 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.
  • Sources indicate that that is embarrassing onstage.
  • In a recent development, most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.

Sources indicate that that is embarrassing onstage. In production, it is a reliability problem: a workflow that succeeded once may fail the next time a user makes the same request. For mission-critical work, such as reconciling a financial transaction or checking a contract for an obligation, that can be a showstopper.

In a recent development, most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average. On AppWorld, a ReAct agent using GPT-4.1 succeeded on 77.4% of runs across five repetitions. But it succeeded in all five runs for only 53.0% of tasks — a 24.4-point consistency gap.

Recent findings suggest that most benchmarks report the first number. We built a way to measure the second — and improve it.

Recent findings suggest that in an earlier post, we introduced ALTK-Evolve — a system that turns an agent's own past trajectories into reusable guidelines, distilled automatically and injected back at inference time. It measurably improves task success, but those results only asked the average-case question too. This post introduces consistency guidelines, a latest guideline type in altk-evolve built on top of a diagnostic tool we call the Consistency Analyzer, that targets this gap directly.

According to recent reports, standard agent evaluation reports Mean@k: run a benchmark k times, average the pass rate. Often k=3, sometimes just 1. It's the number on every leaderboard, and it's what "77% accurate" means in practice.

Mean@k answers "how good is this agent, on average?" It does not answer the question a real user cares about: will it still be good if I ask this exact question again? For that you need Pass^k: the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds on all k runs.

It has been revealed that ⚠️ Pass^k is not Pass@k. The familiar Pass@k is optimistic — it asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeded, the right question when you can verify and retry. Pass^k is its pessimistic mirror image: every attempt must succeed. Same letters, opposite question. Pass^k ≤ Mean@k ≤ Pass@k, always.

A ReAct agent backed by GPT-4.1 posts a Mean@5 of 77.4% — genuinely strong. But Pass^5 is only 53.0%. Nearly a quarter of the benchmark consists of tasks the agent can sometimes solve and sometimes can't, with nothing about the task changing between runs. We call this gap — Mean@k minus Pass^k — the consistency gap.

Industry observers note that this isn't a capability problem you fix with a bigger model. It's an orthogonal axis: an agent can be capable and inconsistent at the same time.

Every time an LLM agent decides something — which API to call, what argument to pass, whether to retry — that decision comes out of a probability distribution over next tokens. What matters is the shape of that distribution. A sharp one puts most of its mass on a single token: the runners-up are far behind, and the same choice comes out run after run. A flat one spreads comparable mass across several near-tied tokens, and which one wins is close to a coin flip.

The shape decides how much noise it takes to change the outcome. Sharp distributions are resilient — GPU floating-point non-associativity, request batching, and other platform-side effects nudge the numbers slightly, but nowhere near enough to reorder a clear winner. Flat distributions are vulnerable to exactly that nudge: near-ties may reorder under small perturbations. And because a trajectory chains dozens of decisions, a small per-step chance of flipping compounds into a large chance that some run goes differently. That's where a 24-point gap comes from.

This is also why the problem survives your decoding settings. Greedy decoding and a fixed seed both govern how a distribution gets turned into a token — they say nothing about the distribution itself. On a hosted endpoint the probabilities shift slightly from run to run, so the same prompt to the same model at temperature zero can still resolve a near-tie one way today and the other way tomorrow.

Our setup: the ReAct agent runs at temperature 0.0, so none of the variance above is ordinary sampling.

Which turns the problem into a search: which steps in a given trajectory were the flat ones — and what do you do about them once you know?

Consistency guidelines come out of a two-stage pipeline that plugs into ALTK-Evolve's existing machinery — with a latest source signal driving what gets written.

Sources indicate that 1. Detect — the Consistency Analyzer. Given one recorded trajectory, the analyzer replays each decision step through controlled resampling, measuring how much the model's output actually varies at that point. Concretely, that's one additional model call per decision step, done once offline — issued with the sampling parameter set to draw k completions at once (k=5 by default) — replayed against the already-recorded context, not upcoming tool calls, not new environment interactions, and not a second end-to-end rollout of the task. This yields a consistency score per decision step that is written into a scorecard to pinpoint exactly which decisions are at risk of flipping on the next run. Detection is fully black-box — no logits, no model internals, no instrumentation beyond the trace you already have.

Sources indicate that 2. Generate — targeted guidelines. Every flagged step becomes a candidate consistency guideline in the standard ALTK-Evolve format, so it slots into the existing storage and retrieval pipeline. Here's a real example, generated by GPT-4.1 from a trajectory of the AppWorld task "How many activities are done in my bucket list as per my SimpleNote note?":.

[Guideline 1] When counting checkbox-style markers in note content, use a line-anchored regex match rather than a plain substring count — note titles often repeat the marker symbol in a legend line.

[Guideline 2] Always verify search results for note queries by checking for multiple matches and confirming the correct note before proceeding.

Nothing here is task-specific trivia. String-counting bugs and unverified search results are decision points that show up with high uncertainty across many AppWorld tasks. That's the point: the analyzer targets instability, not failure — so it catches steps the agent happened to get right this time but could easily get wrong next time.

Watch the 2-minute demo — five parallel runs of the agent split 3-2 on this task because of agent uncertainty about the counting strategy, then run again after these guidelines in context: all five agree.

We evaluated on AppWorld test_normal (168 tasks) with a ReAct agent on GPT-4.1, generating consistency guidelines from a single baseline trajectory per task and testing them on 5 fresh runs.

Mean@5 (%), aggregate — same scale as Pass^5 above.

The consistency gap is cut roughly in half. Aggregate Pass^5 rises 53.0% → 69.0% while Mean@5 rises 77.4% → 81.0%, narrowing the gap between "looks capable" and "can be counted on" from 24.4pp to 12.0pp. Nearly a third of previously-inconsistent tasks become tasks the agent passes on every single run.

In a recent development, the middle and hard tiers gain most. Medium +22.9pp (+44% relative), Hard +14.3pp (+45% relative) — effectively tied in relative terms, with Medium ahead absolutely. Easy gains +12.2pp, having had the least room. This is consistency guidelines doing what they're designed to do: finding and stabilizing the specific decision points where an agent's own uncertainty was leaking into the outcome.

Mean@5 never drops. Preserving average accuracy was a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have: a system that boosts Pass^5 by trading away Mean@5 would just be shifting unreliability around, not fixing it. Mean accuracy holds or improves at every difficulty level.

It has been revealed that applied to a different but related task in the same AppWorld scenario — another variant of the scenario the guidelines were mined from — consistency guidelines still lift Pass^5 by +13.0pp, only 3 points below the same-task number. A guideline derived from one run isn't just patching that run; it's capturing something that transfers.

The sharper evidence comes from a weaker model, gpt-oss-120b. Same-task Pass^5 rose +6.0pp from a much lower baseline (10.1% → 16.1%) — and, interestingly, the similar-task generalization number (+8.7 pp) actually exceeded the same-task gain, suggesting the guidelines were capturing genuinely reusable failure patterns rather than memorizing one trajectory's specifics.

Try the ALTK-Evolve — the open-source repo now includes the Consistency Analyzer and consistency-guideline generation used in these experiments — or read the technical report on arXiv for the complete methodology.

Sources indicate that if accuracy numbers you can't reproduce on your own tasks sound familiar, we'd like to hear about it — concrete examples of flip-prone behavior in your own agents are exactly the kind of feedback that shapes what we build next. Open an concern or a discussion.

Great perspective on agent reliability. Measuring consistency alongside accuracy seems especially vital as AI agents move into workflows where reproducibility matters. The Consistency Analyzer approach is a fascinating way to identify unstable decisions without requiring full task replays.

The useful split is the one most dashboards still refuse to print: Mean@k answers “how good is this agent on average?” Pass^k answers “will the same request still succeed if I ask again?”.

It has been revealed that once you’ve watched a trajectory chain dozens of near-tied tool choices, a strong average with a wide consistency gap is exactly the demo that fails live. Capability and consistency are orthogonal — buying a bigger model can lift Mean without closing the gap.

What I want teams to take from the Consistency Analyzer framing is operational, not the guideline machinery itself: treat flip-prone decision steps as first-class eval targets. One offline resample pass over a recorded trace is a cheaper reliability signal than another end-to-end leaderboard screenshot.

Practical ask for anyone shipping agents from this: do you report Pass^k (even k=3) next to Mean@k in the release gate, and do you refuse the “stable” label when the consistency gap is still large on your hard tier?

It has been revealed that reproducible reliability will not remove disagreement about which guidelines to inject. It will make the disagreement about the right metric.

According to recent reports, thanks, and you've landed on exactly the operational takeaway we hoped for: flip-prone decision steps should be eval targets in their own right. Beyond that, knowing where they are also turns the eval into a diagnostic: a consistency gap tells you that an agent is unreliable, while the flip-prone steps tell you where and why.

On your release-gate question: we'd strongly encourage it, and k=3 is a sensible default. A few things we'd suggest to anyone adopting Pass^k as a gate:.

I'd like to understand your closing point better. In our experiments, we didn't choose among individual guidelines: for each upcoming task, we injected the guidelines derived from the most similar task. I'm curious where you see the disagreement about which guidelines to inject arising.

Prop firms, meanwhile, can oversee evaluations and funded accounts, as well as configure bespoke rules and drawdown limits.

Industry observers note that an ArcaTrader spokesperson noted, “Every major market has a platform the industry defaults to. We’ve run this platform for real traders inside our own business for more than two years, so we know what brokers and prop firms actually need.
